Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN)  -- The Taliban in Afghanistan have momentum that makes any effort to negotiate with them difficult, the U.S. defense secretary said. Defense Secretary Robert Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday. He's visiting Afghanistan on Wednesday. Secretary Robert Gates spoke to CNN's Chris Lawrence in an exclusive interview Tuesday evening before leaving for Afghanistan, where he is visiting troops and bases Wednesday. "The political level of the Taliban probably isn't ready to think about reconciliation or any kind of accommodation at this point," Gates said in the interview. "They probably feel like they have the momentum with them. And until that momentum changes, it will be difficult." As part of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, the military and Afghanistan government are attempting to reach out to elements of the Taliban who are engaged in the battle for financial gain, rather than ideological gain. "There are really two groups we're talking about -- the younger, or less committed, who do this mainly to earn a living and put food on the table for their families, and those that are more ideologically committed. The latter are going to be a tougher pull, and we'll probably have to wait awhile before there's an opportunity there." On Monday, CNN's Nic Robertson interviewed a spokesman for the Taliban, Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the Taliban will only negotiate with the Afghanistan government when the United States leaves the country. "Our conditions are clear, we want to negotiate and they [the U.S.] will not interfere in our affairs; secondly, they [the U.S.] will leave the country," Mujahid told CNN. Gates said the stance was not surprising. "Well I don't know what else he'd say. He's leading the opposition, he's leading this insurgency. He's not going to sort of, sort of throw down and say 'We're ready to negotiate, we're about done here,' " Gates said. The United States is adding 21,000 troops to the Afghanistan battlefield. The majority will be moving to the south to confront the Taliban along the porous Pakistani border. The Taliban have had mostly free rein in that area with few U.S. or coalition forces to confront them until now. Gates admitted moving the battle to the south will mean there is "a tough fight ahead." "I think, certainly, I have been pretty clear. As we move into areas of the south that have not seen any Afghan or coalition forces so far, we're clearly going to be going into areas where the Taliban are very entrenched," he said. "And, sad to say, I expect with the rising level of our activity and operations, there probably will be higher casualties." In recent weeks, the Pakistani government has seen the Taliban gain control on its side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Privately, Pakistani officials have expressed concern to the United States that the increased fighting in southern Afghanistan will only push the Taliban back to the Pakistani side. "Well I think it's just the reality that there are extremists on both sides of that border. And they threaten both the elected government of Afghanistan and the elected government of Pakistan. So like it or not, they both have a certain common enemy," Gates said. Gates said he is encouraged by recent cooperation efforts between the two countries to deal with the problem, and by Pakistan's recent confrontation with the Taliban in Bunir province, near the capital of Islamabad. "The signs right now are pretty positive," he told CNN.

outputs.L1:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN) — The Taliban in Afghanistan have gained momentum that is making any effort to negotiate with them difficult, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said.

Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday and is scheduled to visit Afghanistan on Wednesday. He spoke with CNN’s Chris Lawrence in an exclusive interview Tuesday evening before departing for Afghanistan, where he will visit troops and bases.

“The political level of the Taliban probably isn’t ready to think about reconciliation or any kind of accommodation at this point,” Gates said in the interview. “They probably feel like they have the momentum with them. And until that momentum changes, it will be difficult.”

As part of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, the military and the Afghan government are attempting to reach out to elements of the Taliban who are engaged in the fighting for financial gain rather than ideological reasons.

“There are really two groups we’re talking about—the younger, or less committed, who do this mainly to earn a living and put food on the table for their families, and those that are more ideologically committed,” Gates said. “The latter are going to be a tougher pull, and we’ll probably have to wait awhile before there’s an opportunity there.”

On Monday, CNN’s Nic Robertson interviewed Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the Taliban would negotiate with the Afghan government only when the United States leaves the country.

“Our conditions are clear: we want to negotiate, and they [the U.S.] will not interfere in our affairs; secondly, they [the U.S.] will leave the country,” Mujahid told CNN.

Gates said the stance was not surprising.

“Well, I don’t know what else he’d say. He’s leading the opposition, he’s leading this insurgency. He’s not going to sort of, sort of throw down and say, ‘We’re ready to negotiate, we’re about done here,’” Gates said.

The United States is adding 21,000 troops to the Afghan battlefield. The majority will be deployed to the south to confront the Taliban along the porous Pakistani border. Until now, the Taliban have had mostly free rein in that area, with few U.S. or coalition forces present to confront them.

Gates acknowledged that moving the battle to the south will mean there is “a tough fight ahead.”

“I think, certainly, I have been pretty clear. As we move into areas of the south that have not seen any Afghan or coalition forces so far, we’re clearly going to be going into areas where the Taliban are very entrenched,” he said. “And, sad to say, I expect with the rising level of our activity and operations, there probably will be higher casualties.”

In recent weeks, the Pakistani government has seen the Taliban gain control on its side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Privately, Pakistani officials have expressed concern to the United States that increased fighting in southern Afghanistan will only push the Taliban back to the Pakistani side.

“Well, I think it’s just the reality that there are extremists on both sides of that border. And they threaten both the elected government of Afghanistan and the elected government of Pakistan. So, like it or not, they both have a certain common enemy,” Gates said.

Gates said he is encouraged by recent cooperation efforts between the two countries to address the problem, as well as by Pakistan’s recent confrontation with the Taliban in Bunir province, near the capital, Islamabad.

“The signs right now are pretty positive,” he told CNN.

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN) — U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the Taliban’s current strength in Afghanistan is making prospects for talks with the group difficult.

Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday and was scheduled to travel to Afghanistan on Wednesday. Before departing, he gave an exclusive interview Tuesday evening to CNN’s Chris Lawrence. During his Afghanistan visit, Gates planned to meet with troops and visit military bases.

“At the political level, the Taliban probably is not yet prepared to consider reconciliation or any form of compromise,” Gates said. “They likely believe the momentum is on their side. Until that shifts, negotiations will be hard.”

As part of the American approach in Afghanistan, U.S. military officials and the Afghan government are trying to connect with Taliban members who are fighting for money rather than because of ideology.

Gates described two broad categories within the movement: younger or less dedicated fighters who join mainly to make a living and support their families, and others who are more deeply driven by ideology. He said the second group would be much harder to draw away, and that it may take time before there is any real opening with them.

On Monday, CNN’s Nic Robertson interviewed Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the Taliban would negotiate with the Afghan government only if the United States withdrew from Afghanistan.

“Our conditions are clear,” Mujahid told CNN. “We want to negotiate, and they [the U.S.] must not interfere in our affairs. Second, they [the U.S.] must leave the country.”

Gates said he was not surprised by that position.

“I don’t know what else he would say,” Gates said. “He is leading the opposition, he is leading the insurgency. He is not going to simply give up and say, ‘We are ready to talk; we are basically finished here.’”

The United States is sending an additional 21,000 troops to the Afghan battlefield. Most of them are expected to deploy to the south, where they will confront Taliban forces near the difficult-to-control border with Pakistan. Until now, the Taliban have operated in much of that region with little challenge from U.S. or coalition troops.

Gates acknowledged that shifting more combat operations into southern Afghanistan means “a tough fight ahead.”

“I have been very clear about this,” he said. “As we move into southern areas that so far have not had Afghan or coalition forces present, we will be entering places where the Taliban are strongly established. Unfortunately, as our operations and activity increase, I expect casualties will probably rise as well.”

In recent weeks, Pakistan’s government has watched the Taliban expand control on the Pakistani side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Pakistani officials have privately told the United States they are worried that heavier fighting in southern Afghanistan could drive Taliban fighters back across the border into Pakistan.

Gates said the situation reflects the fact that extremists operate on both sides of the frontier.

“They threaten both Afghanistan’s elected government and Pakistan’s elected government,” he said. “So whether they like it or not, the two countries share a common enemy.”

Gates added that he was encouraged by recent cooperation between Afghanistan and Pakistan in confronting the issue, as well as by Pakistan’s recent action against the Taliban in Bunir province, located near the capital, Islamabad.

“The signs right now are pretty positive,” Gates told CNN.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the Taliban’s current battlefield momentum makes serious negotiations or reconciliation difficult. According to Gates, the movement’s political leadership is unlikely to consider any form of accommodation as long as it believes it is gaining strength or maintaining an advantage.

Gates suggested that a shift in momentum would be necessary before the Taliban’s senior leaders might be willing to enter meaningful talks. Until then, he said, they are likely to see little reason to compromise with the Afghan government or its international partners.

At the same time, the United States and the Afghan government are attempting to reach out to lower-level Taliban fighters who may not be deeply committed to the group’s ideology. Officials believe some insurgents fight primarily for financial reasons or local grievances, rather than strong political or religious conviction. These fighters may be more open to reconciliation if offered security, employment, or a way to reintegrate into Afghan society.

Gates said the situation is different for Taliban members who are ideologically committed to the movement. He warned that persuading these individuals would be far more difficult and could take significantly longer. In his view, meaningful negotiations with the Taliban’s most committed elements may not be possible until they believe continued fighting will not bring them success.

A Taliban spokesman, however, said the group would only consider negotiations with the Afghan government if the United States withdraws from Afghanistan and ends what the Taliban describes as interference in the country’s affairs.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said that the Taliban’s recent battlefield momentum is making efforts at reconciliation more difficult, even as the United States and the Afghan government continue to pursue a strategy aimed at drawing lower-level fighters away from the insurgency. Gates said many Taliban members are not driven primarily by ideology, but by money, local grievances, intimidation, or a lack of other opportunities. Because of that, he suggested, some fighters may be persuaded to lay down their weapons if they are offered security, employment, and a place in Afghan society.

At the same time, Gates cautioned that broader political negotiations with senior Taliban leaders are unlikely to succeed while the insurgency believes it is gaining strength. He argued that groups with momentum on the battlefield have little incentive to compromise, making serious reconciliation difficult until the balance of power changes. In his view, the Taliban must first be weakened militarily and convinced that it cannot win through force.

That assessment helps explain the U.S. decision to send additional troops to Afghanistan and intensify efforts against Taliban forces. The strategy is intended not only to protect Afghan civilians and strengthen the Afghan government, but also to reduce the insurgency’s confidence and create conditions in which political outreach might become more effective. Gates emphasized that reconciliation remains an important part of the overall approach, but said it is most likely to work only after military pressure has shifted the momentum away from the Taliban.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Defense Secretary Robert Gates saying the Taliban have momentum in Afghanistan and that negotiations will be difficult, including his comments before visiting Afghanistan and the planned U.S. troop increase.
counterfactuals.output:
**Gates: Taliban has momentum in Afghanistan, talks will be difficult**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the Taliban has gained momentum in Afghanistan and warned that any effort to negotiate with insurgent elements would be difficult and unlikely to produce quick results.

Speaking to reporters before a visit to Afghanistan, Gates said the United States and its allies face a serious challenge as violence has increased and Taliban fighters have expanded their influence in parts of the country.

“The Taliban do have the momentum right now,” Gates said, according to his remarks to journalists traveling with him. He added that reversing those gains would require a stronger military presence, better governance and continued pressure on insurgent networks.

Gates’ comments came as the United States prepared to increase the number of American troops in Afghanistan. The planned deployment is intended to bolster security, particularly in the country’s south and east, where Taliban activity has intensified and NATO forces have struggled to hold territory.

U.S. commanders have requested additional combat forces to help secure population centers, disrupt Taliban supply routes and support Afghan army and police units. The troop increase is also expected to provide security ahead of Afghan political developments and to give U.S. and coalition forces more flexibility in counterinsurgency operations.

Gates said the United States remains open to reconciliation efforts with insurgents who are willing to renounce violence and accept the Afghan government, but he cautioned that broad negotiations with the Taliban leadership would be complicated.

He said talks would be hard because the Taliban is not a single unified movement and includes hard-line leaders, local fighters, criminal networks and groups with ties to al Qaeda. Any political outreach, Gates suggested, would need to distinguish between reconcilable elements and militants committed to overthrowing the Afghan government.

The defense secretary’s trip to Afghanistan was expected to include meetings with U.S. commanders, coalition officials and Afghan leaders. His visit comes amid a reassessment of U.S. strategy in the war, which has increasingly shifted from Iraq back to Afghanistan as the central front in the fight against extremist groups.

Gates said the troop increase alone would not be enough to stabilize Afghanistan. He emphasized that military gains must be matched by improvements in Afghan governance, economic development and efforts to reduce corruption.

The Taliban, ousted from power by U.S.-led forces in 2001, has re-emerged as a resilient insurgency. In recent years, militants have carried out more roadside bombings, ambushes and attacks on Afghan officials, coalition troops and civilians.

U.S. officials have said the additional troops are meant to regain the initiative and create conditions for the Afghan government to expand its authority. But Gates’ remarks underscored the difficulty of the mission and the administration’s concern that the war could worsen without a substantial shift in strategy.

counterfactuals.output:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said in an exclusive interview with CNN that efforts to reconcile with elements of the Taliban remain at an early stage and are unlikely to succeed until insurgents believe they can no longer win on the battlefield.

Speaking with CNN’s Chris Lawrence, Gates said the Afghan government’s outreach to Taliban fighters could eventually help end the war, but he cautioned that meaningful negotiations would depend on sustained military pressure from U.S., NATO and Afghan forces.

Gates said the aim is to persuade lower- and mid-level Taliban members — and possibly some senior figures — to lay down their arms, accept the Afghan constitution and break ties with al Qaeda. But he emphasized that reconciliation cannot be based on concessions that would allow the Taliban to regain control or provide sanctuary to terrorist groups.

The defense secretary also addressed the continuing challenge along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, where insurgents have long used remote areas as safe havens. Gates said Pakistan has taken important steps against militant groups inside its territory, but he acknowledged that cross-border movement remains a serious problem for coalition forces in Afghanistan.

Gates said closer cooperation between Kabul, Islamabad and Washington is essential to reducing militant activity in the border region. He noted that progress in Afghanistan depends not only on military operations inside the country but also on limiting the ability of Taliban fighters to regroup and resupply across the frontier.

In the interview, Gates also warned that U.S. and coalition casualties are likely to rise as more troops move into contested areas and intensify operations against insurgents. He said the increase would be painful but expected, particularly as forces push into Taliban strongholds and expand security efforts meant to protect Afghan civilians.

Gates said the coming months would be difficult, but he argued that the strategy depends on demonstrating to Afghans that their government and international forces can provide lasting security. He said that pressure on the Taliban, combined with political outreach and improved Afghan governance, remains central to the U.S.-led war effort.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the latest U.S. military strategy in Afghanistan in the style of a CNN dispatch, focusing on Gates’ remarks about Taliban negotiations, insurgents motivated by money versus ideology, and Pakistan’s concerns.
counterfactuals.output:
**Washington —** The U.S. military strategy in Afghanistan, as described by Defense Secretary Robert Gates, centered on intensifying pressure on the Taliban while leaving the door open to eventual political reconciliation.

Gates said negotiations with elements of the Taliban could be part of a long-term solution, but only after coalition and Afghan forces weakened the insurgency enough to shift the battlefield momentum. He drew a distinction between hard-line Taliban leaders driven by ideology and lower-level fighters who, he said, were often motivated by money, local grievances or lack of alternatives.

The strategy, in that view, was to peel away those “reconcilable” insurgents through security gains, economic incentives and Afghan-led outreach, while continuing military operations against committed extremists and al Qaeda-linked elements.

Pakistan remained a central concern. U.S. officials recognized that Islamabad viewed Afghan reconciliation through the lens of its own security interests, especially fears of Indian influence in Afghanistan and concerns about being sidelined in any talks with Taliban factions. Gates’ remarks reflected Washington’s effort to reassure Pakistan while pressing it to do more against insurgent safe havens along the border.

The overall approach combined military escalation, Afghan government outreach and regional diplomacy — with the goal of weakening the Taliban enough to make negotiations possible on U.S. and Afghan terms.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a full-length CNN article based on an interview with U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates in which he says the Taliban are not ready for reconciliation because they believe they have momentum.
counterfactuals.output:
**Gates: Taliban not ready for reconciliation because they believe they have momentum**

**By CNN Staff**

**WASHINGTON —** U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the Taliban are not yet prepared to enter serious reconciliation talks with the Afghan government, arguing that insurgent leaders still believe they have momentum on the battlefield and can wait out the United States and its allies.

In an interview, Gates said the prospects for a political settlement in Afghanistan depend heavily on changing the Taliban’s calculation — convincing its leaders that they cannot win militarily and that continued fighting will not improve their position.

“The Taliban believe they have the momentum,” Gates said, explaining why he does not think senior insurgent figures are ready for meaningful negotiations. Until that perception changes, he suggested, reconciliation efforts are unlikely to produce a significant breakthrough.

The comments come as the United States and NATO continue a major counterinsurgency campaign in Afghanistan aimed at reversing Taliban gains, strengthening Afghan security forces and creating conditions for a political process that could eventually end the war.

Gates drew a distinction between lower-level Taliban fighters who might be persuaded to lay down their weapons and reintegrate into Afghan society, and senior Taliban leaders who remain committed to the insurgency. The former, he indicated, may be more open to offers of jobs, protection and a return to their communities. The latter, he said, are unlikely to reconcile unless they face sustained military pressure.

U.S. officials have long said there is no purely military solution to the war in Afghanistan, but they have also insisted that reconciliation must take place from a position of strength. Gates’ remarks underscored that view: The battlefield, he said, will shape the negotiating table.

The Obama administration has backed Afghan-led efforts to encourage defections from the insurgency and explore the possibility of talks with Taliban elements willing to renounce violence, cut ties with al Qaeda and accept the Afghan constitution. But officials have remained cautious about the chances of reaching a near-term agreement with the Taliban’s top leadership.

Gates said the key question is whether the insurgency can be made to understand that time is not on its side. For years, Taliban commanders have sought to portray the United States and NATO as weary and divided, betting that Western forces will eventually leave and that the Afghan government will be too weak to survive without them.

That perception has complicated U.S. strategy. American commanders have argued that additional troops and expanded operations are needed not only to secure population centers but also to demonstrate to insurgents that they cannot simply wait out the coalition.

The defense secretary’s assessment reflects a central challenge for Washington: pursuing a political end to the war while continuing combat operations designed to weaken the Taliban enough to make negotiations viable.

Afghan President Hamid Karzai has repeatedly called for reconciliation with insurgents who are willing to stop fighting and accept the authority of the Afghan state. His government has supported programs intended to bring foot soldiers back into local communities, but talks with senior Taliban figures have been halting, uncertain and often difficult to verify.

The Taliban, meanwhile, have publicly rejected negotiations under conditions set by Kabul and Washington, insisting that foreign troops must leave Afghanistan. U.S. officials have dismissed any demand for an immediate withdrawal as unrealistic, while emphasizing that an eventual transition to Afghan security control remains the goal.

Gates said reconciliation cannot succeed if the Taliban believe they are negotiating from a position of strength. The purpose of the ongoing military campaign, he indicated, is to change that dynamic.

The United States has increased pressure on Taliban strongholds in southern and eastern Afghanistan, while also working to expand and train Afghan army and police forces. The hope, according to U.S. officials, is that improved security and stronger Afghan institutions will reduce the Taliban’s influence and open political space for a settlement.

Still, Gates’ remarks suggested that Washington does not expect quick results. Even as U.S. leaders discuss a path toward transition, they face the reality that the Taliban remain resilient in many areas and continue to test the Afghan government’s reach.

For Gates, the issue is not whether reconciliation will eventually be necessary, but whether the Taliban have reached the point where they see it as necessary.

At the moment, he said, they have not.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a news story including quotes from Robert Gates and Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid about possible negotiations, U.S. troops moving into southern Afghanistan, and cooperation between Afghanistan and Pakistan.
counterfactuals.output:
**Gates Says Afghan Talks Possible as U.S. Shifts Forces South**

*KABUL, Afghanistan —* U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said possible negotiations with elements of the Taliban could become part of a broader effort to stabilize Afghanistan, even as American troops prepare to move in greater numbers into the country’s volatile south.

Speaking amid rising violence and growing concern over insurgent sanctuaries along the Afghan-Pakistan border, Gates said military pressure alone would not end the war. “There has to be ultimately — and I’ll underscore ultimately — reconciliation as part of a political outcome,” Gates said, while stressing that any talks would have to be led by the Afghan government.

Gates said the United States would continue expanding its military presence in southern Afghanistan, where Taliban influence remains strongest. The additional troops, he said, are intended to improve security, protect local communities and create conditions under which political outreach might be possible.

Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid dismissed the prospect of negotiations under current conditions, saying talks could not take place while foreign forces remain in Afghanistan. “As long as foreign troops are in our country, real negotiations are not possible,” Mujahid said. He added that the Taliban would continue fighting what it calls an occupation.

Afghan officials have repeatedly said they are open to dialogue with insurgents who renounce violence, accept the Afghan constitution and sever ties with extremist groups. But the Taliban has publicly rejected those conditions, and violence has continued to spread, particularly in Helmand, Kandahar and neighboring southern provinces.

Gates also emphasized the need for closer cooperation between Afghanistan and Pakistan, saying insurgent networks operating across the border pose a threat to both countries. He said improved intelligence sharing, tighter border coordination and joint efforts against militant safe havens would be essential to any long-term peace.

“The problems on one side of the border affect the other,” Gates said. “Afghanistan and Pakistan both have an interest in preventing extremists from using the border region as a base.”

Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have often been strained, with Afghan leaders accusing Pakistan of not doing enough to stop Taliban fighters from crossing into Afghanistan. Pakistan has denied supporting insurgents and says it has suffered heavily from militant attacks on its own soil.

Analysts say the combination of a larger U.S. troop presence, possible political outreach and regional cooperation reflects a shifting strategy as the conflict enters another difficult phase. But with the Taliban rejecting talks and violence intensifying in the south, prospects for a negotiated settlement remain uncertain.
